extracted.intended_audience: authors and writers (particularly novelists/genre writers) seeking practical advice on promoting books and building readership
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors on smart, sustainable promotion of books: choosing channels, owning assets, building community, and balancing time between promotion and writing. Emphasizes long-term strategies (website, newsletter, reader-focused platforms) and realistic awareness of paid advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write your next thing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotion revolutions happen constantly; tactics that work for a time will often stop working. The only consistent, dependable investment is continuing to produce new work. If you aren't consistently working on the next thing, you'll be vulnerable when promotional channels change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own your online home (domain and server)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your brand, your identity online, needs to have a home that you own: your domain name, your server, your blog posts or photos or comics or whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let third-party platforms be your primary, irreplaceable home because they can cut you off or disappear. Keep a website you control; refuse publisher requests that would put your primary presence on a publisher-owned series site (reject sites that brand the series instead of you).

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a solid website with a newsletter sign-up you control
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure to have a solid website with a newsletter sign-up that you are keeping up-to-date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual websites get fewer hits than social media, a site you control cannot be taken away. Keep it updated and use it as the authoritative home for your author identity. When publishers offer to build series websites, negotiate instead to keep traffic on your author site and use publisher funds for shared marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use newsletters as a primary, controllable promotional tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsletters are one of the most valuable resources — people opt in and want to hear when you have new work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a smaller list than social followers but a much higher engagement (Brandon cites ~30–40% response rates as common). Set them up properly (MailChimp or similar), avoid spammy tactics, send at reasonable cadence (quarterly recommended), give subscribers exclusive content (fiction excerpts, previews, promotions) and treat them with respect so they become evangelists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect opt-in and avoid spammy newsletter practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Be upfront with your newsletter and not have one of those big pop-ups and not just automatically sign people up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid aggressive or deceptive sign-up practices that annoy readers or trigger spam filters. Provide clear value and exclusive material so subscribers welcome your messages and spread word-of-mouth rather than unsubscribe or mark you as spam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to how readers find books (not only where writers congregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to the way readers are finding out about books, not just where writers congregate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a reader and a writer, consider whether you would discover your own book by the channels you use. If the answer is no, change tactics. Platforms where writers hang out (e.g., Twitter) may not be where prospective readers discover recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-of-mouth and being 'on the lips' of your desired audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Word-of-mouth is one of the most powerful promotional tools; get people talking about your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to be mentioned alongside authors/readers you want to be compared with. Consider what those other authors do to generate conversation and emulate effective techniques. Being recommended by others (readers, other authors) creates much more credible promotion than self-promotion alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick social platforms where readers are discussing your books and you can produce good content
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick the places where people are talking about your books, and platforms that you find easy to use; pick the areas where you can write good content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency is more valuable than being on the most popular platform. Don't spread yourself thin; choose platforms where (a) discussion about your genre/book happens and (b) you can post consistently high-quality content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be part of the discussion, don't just broadcast
rubrics_metrics.description: You want to be part of the discussion; the social aspect of it is key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with readers and other creators, amplify praise (retweet/reshare endorsements), respond to comments, and participate in community conversations rather than only pushing announcements. Social amplification by others is more persuasive than self-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the purpose of each social presence (platform-building vs serving existing readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different social media presences have different goals: platform-building (attracting new readers) vs informing/serving existing readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what each account is for. Established authors may use social channels primarily to inform current readers; others may try to build a platform by posting more broadly appealing content. Tailor tone and content strategy to that goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research comparable authors and emulate effective tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at authors who self-promote, and how they're doing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze authors you want to be compared with: their scale, responses, platforms, and tactics. Group them by sales/awareness and learn what earns engagement. Use those observations to design a strategy appropriate to your stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target your promotion; don't try to be everywhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Find where the discussions about your books are happening and focus there; being consistent matters more than trying to reach every platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New social platforms may attract new people; legacy platforms often retain the same user base. Avoid trying to maintain a presence on all platforms; instead pick ones you can be consistent on and that reach your intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community platforms to create ongoing conversations (Discord, Reddit, Twitch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create spaces (e.g., Discord) where fans can continue conversations after events so some become evangelists and do marketing for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link ephemeral live-event chats (Twitch chat) into persistent communities (Discord) so fans can continue interacting. Participate in community-specific spaces (Reddit AMAs/threads) where you can share updates in ways that feel native and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about pay-to-play advertising and measure ROI
rubrics_metrics.description: Book marketing has become pay to play; many major social platforms and Amazon now require paid promotion to get eyeballs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand current advertising costs and expected returns (the podcast cites indie authors spending five- to six-figures to market books). Factor advertising spend into revenue expectations and be cautious about unsustainable ad-driven strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on transient promotional channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional tools come and go (e.g., book blogs, local bookstore hand-delivery used to work but are less effective now).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't build your entire strategy on a single channel that may decline. Diversify, prioritize owned channels (website/newsletter), and monitor shifts so you can pivot when a channel becomes ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exclusive content and promotions to reward and engage fans
rubrics_metrics.description: Give newsletter subscribers and fans something exclusive (exclusive fiction, previews, special promotions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive content increases perceived value of subscribing and encourages retention and sharing. Use promotions thoughtfully to reward core fans rather than mass freebie spamming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of frequency and quality when communicating
rubrics_metrics.description: Being consistent (regular updates) and producing good content on chosen channels matters more than quantity across channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a realistic cadence (Brandon suggests at least quarterly newsletters) and stick to it. Quality content that fits the medium is more effective than frequent low-value noise.
